props.title: Bestiaire

sections.content: **Bestiaire** (2012) represents a fascinating evolution in observational documentary filmmaking, following in the contemplative tradition of films like Le Quattro Volte (2010) and Sweetgrass (2009). Director Denis Côté strips away conventional documentary elements - there's no narration, no interviews, no music - to create an unflinching study of the relationship between humans and captive animals at a Quebec safari park. The film's patient, static shots echo Frederick Wiseman's institutional studies while pushing further into pure visual meditation.

sections.content: Côté's approach builds on a rich tradition of nature documentaries that challenge conventional wildlife film techniques. While mainstream works like **March of the Penguins** (2005) use narrative and anthropomorphization, films like **Bestiaire** and **La Quatre Volte** strip away these familiar frameworks. The results are more challenging but ultimately more honest about our complicated relationship with the animal world. Microcosmos (1996) pioneered this approach, letting intimate insect footage speak for itself without imposed narrative.

The confined spaces of **Bestiaire** create an intentionally uncomfortable parallel with earlier films about human institutions. **Titicut Follies** (1967) exposed a mental hospital's dehumanizing conditions through similar observational techniques. Both films raise questions about containment and control without explicit commentary. This connects to later works like Our Daily Bread (2005), which uses fixed camera positions to examine industrial food production's treatment of animals. sections.content: The impact of **Bestiaire** can be seen in subsequent nature documentaries that embrace similar minimalist approaches. **Leviathan** (2012) uses immersive camera techniques to capture commercial fishing with no narrative framework. **The Velvet Queen** (2021) spends long, quiet moments waiting for glimpses of snow leopards, prioritizing patience over spectacle. These films represent a growing movement away from the polished presentation of BBC nature documentaries toward rawer, more challenging visions.
